title: Conceived without sin
hook: Catholics teach that Mary was kept free of original sin from her first moment (defined 1854, CCC 491)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anne and Joachim, Mary's parents in the old story; Anne is the English form of Hannah, grace. Your line was someone raised her too.

A quick quiz. What is the Immaculate Conception? A common answer: Jesus being conceived without a human father. Good guess. Wrong event. That's the virgin birth, a different teaching. The Immaculate Conception is about Mary's conception: her beginning, in her mother Anne's womb, conceived the ordinary way, by two parents, and something the Church says was different about that ordinary beginning. On December eighth, 1854, Pope Pius the Ninth defined it as a teaching of the faith.

Catholics believe every human being comes into the world carrying original sin: a wound from the beginning, a nature already tilted away from God. The Immaculate Conception says that Mary, from the very first moment of her existence, was kept free of it. Immaculate means without stain. And here's the careful part the Church insists on: this wasn't because Mary earned it, or because she didn't need saving. The Catechism says it was a singular grace, given in view of what her son would do. A medieval friar named Duns Scotus argued that keeping someone from falling is a rescue too, and a finer one. Teachers often picture it as a pit. You can pull someone out after they fall in, or you can catch them at the edge. Both are rescues. Mary, in this picture, was caught. Where does it come from? Catholics point to the angel's greeting, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." In Greek, full of grace is a single word, a verb form for something already done whose effect lasts: graced, and still graced. Catholic writers read it as a hint that grace was in her from the start, God preparing a mother for his son. Christians hold this differently. Orthodox Christians call Mary all-holy but don't define her conception this way, and Protestant churches don't make it a teaching of the faith. For Catholics it's a feast, December eighth, and a holy day.
screen: `IMMACULATE: WITHOUT STAIN.` · `KEPT FREE FROM THE FIRST MOMENT.` · `CAUGHT BEFORE THE FALL.` · `FULL OF GRACE, AND STILL FULL.` · then, large: `PREPARED FROM THE START.`

segments.voice: Think back to something good in your life that someone set up before you arrived: a name picked out, a room painted, money saved, a door held open years before you walked through it. Let yourself notice how much was ready for you. If you pray, you can say the angel's words slowly, once: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee.
Immaculate Conception. Mary, kept free of original sin from her first moment, by grace, in view of her son. Not the virgin birth. Today's word.
Your line: prepared from the start. Not the virgin birth: Mary's own beginning. That's day seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Immaculate Conception on 8 December, a holy day of obligation in many countries, and the United States has Mary under this title as its patroness.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 1:28 given from memory (matches the Catholic day 10/14 usage); confirm.
Ineffabilis Deus, 8 December 1854; CCC 491–492 ('by a singular grace and privilege... in view of the merits of Jesus Christ'). Paraphrased.
Duns Scotus's argument (preservative redemption) given as a picture of a pit; the picture is a common teaching illustration, not Scotus's own words. Confirm phrasing.
Lourdes, 25 March 1858: Bernadette reported the words 'Que soy era Immaculada Councepciou' in Occitan/Gascon. Confirm.
Orthodox and Protestant positions summarized briefly without ranking; Orthodox views vary, many reject the dogma as framed with Western original-sin theology. Confirm fairness.
Patroness of the United States under this title (1847). 8 December is a holy day of obligation in the US. Confirm.
